current:
What happens when you click Run: counts are rescaled to CPM (counts per million) so dishes are comparable; each gene's average in Group B (differentiated) is divided by its average in Group A (undifferentiated) to give a log₂ fold change. If both groups have at least two dishes, a Welch t-test on log₂(CPM+1) gives a p-value per gene, corrected for testing thousands of genes at once (Benjamini–Hochberg). That's a simplified classroom version of what DESeq2 does: good for learning, not for publishing.

Expect fewer hits than a real tool. With only 2–3 dishes per group a t-test can never produce a very small p-value (there is too little information), and after correcting for ~12,000 genes only the strongest changes survive. Real tools like DESeq2 get more power by sharing information across genes. If a gene looks obviously different but comes out "not significant", that is usually this limitation, not evidence the gene is unchanged.

current: RNA-seq: what is actually being measured?
raw: RNA-seq: what is actually being measured?

current: Every cell constantly copies its active genes into RNA. RNA-seq collects all of that RNA, reads it, and counts how many reads came from each gene. More reads = the gene is more "on". It's a snapshot of what the cell is doing, not what it could do.
raw: Every cell constantly copies its active genes into RNA. RNA-seq collects all of that RNA, reads it, and counts how many reads came from each gene. More reads = the gene is more "on". It's a snapshot of what the cell is doing, not what it could do.

current: CPM: counts per million
raw: CPM: counts per million

current: Different dishes get different numbers of total reads (one might have 15 million, another 3 million). To compare fairly, each gene's count is scaled to "per million reads". CPM is the number on the y-axis of the gene chart. Roughly: under 1 = basically off, 10–100 = solidly on, 1000+ = a heavy hitter.

current: Replicates: why the number of dots matters
raw: Replicates: why the number of dots matters

current: A replicate is an independent dish treated the same way. Replicates tell you how much a gene wobbles naturally. With several dishes per condition we can ask "is the difference bigger than the wobble?" That's a statistical test. With only one dish per condition there's no wobble to measure, so we can only describe a difference, not test it. The undifferentiated-vs-differentiated dataset is exactly that situation.
raw: A replicate is an independent dish treated the same way. Replicates tell you how much a gene wobbles naturally. With several dishes per condition we can ask "is the difference bigger than the wobble?" That's a statistical test. With only one dish per condition there's no wobble to measure, so we can only describe a difference, not test it. The undifferentiated-vs-differentiated dataset is exactly that situation.

current: log₂ fold change: the "how much" number
raw: log₂ fold change: the "how much" number

current: Fold change is the ratio: treated ÷ control. We take log₂ so up and down are symmetric: +1 = doubled, +2 = 4×, +3 = 8×; −1 = halved, −3 = one-eighth. A log₂FC of −3.5 means the gene dropped to about 1/11th of its starting level.
raw: Fold change is the ratio: treated ÷ control. We take log₂ so up and down are symmetric: +1 = doubled, +2 = 4×, +3 = 8×; −1 = halved, −3 = one-eighth. A log₂FC of −3.5 means the gene dropped to about 1/11th of its starting level.

current: p-value and adjusted p-value: the "how sure" number
raw: p-value and adjusted p-value: the "how sure" number

current: A p-value is the chance you'd see a difference this big by luck if nothing were really going on. Small = convincing. But we test ~13,000 genes at once, so some will look convincing by luck alone. The adjusted p-value (also called FDR) corrects for that. We call a gene "significant" when adjusted p < 0.05 and it changed at least 2× (|log₂FC| > 1).

But we test ~13,000 genes at once, so some will look convincing by luck alone. The adjusted p-value (also called FDR) corrects for that. We call a gene "significant" when adjusted p < 0.05 and it changed at least 2× (|log₂FC| > 1).

current: DESeq2 vs the t-test used for your own data
raw: DESeq2 vs the t-test used for your own data

current: DESeq2 is the standard tool for asking "which genes really changed?" It models count noise carefully and borrows information across genes, which makes it reliable even with few replicates. The Welch t-test this page runs on uploaded data is a simpler cousin: it compares the two groups' averages relative to their spread, gene by gene. It captures the idea, and it's what you'd learn in an intro stats course, but for a real paper you'd use DESeq2 or edgeR.

It captures the idea, and it's what you'd learn in an intro stats course, but for a real paper you'd use DESeq2 or edgeR.

current: Left–right is effect size, up is confidence. The shape looks like an erupting volcano because big changes tend to be confident changes. You only get a volcano when there are replicates to compute p-values from.

raw: Batch effect: why samples from different runs need care

current: Samples processed on different days, by different hands, or on different sequencing runs pick up small systematic differences that have nothing to do with biology. When two conditions were sequenced separately, some of their difference could be batch, not treatment. Big, biologically coherent changes are still informative; small ones aren't.

current: Differentiation: what "undifferentiated vs differentiated" means
raw: Differentiation: what "undifferentiated vs differentiated" means

current: CAD cells can be kept dividing in a stem-like state, or nudged (by removing serum) to stop dividing and grow long neuron-like processes. That switch, from a proliferating cell to a mature, specialised neuron, is called differentiation, and it rewires thousands of genes: division genes go quiet, neuron-identity genes switch on.

current: CAD cells: what are they?
raw: CAD cells: what are they?

current: CAD cells are a mouse line derived from Cath.a cells, a central-nervous-system catecholaminergic line, the kind of neuron that makes dopamine and noradrenaline. In serum they divide; in serum-free media they stop dividing and grow neurite-like processes. That makes them a convenient, cheap model for asking what happens as a neuron matures, without needing animals.
